Please help [improve it](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Anonymous_matching&action=edit) by removing [less pertinent examples](/wiki/Wikipedia:Example_cruft "Wikipedia:Example cruft") and [elaborating](/wiki/Wikipedia:PROSE "Wikipedia:PROSE") on existing ones. *(September 2018)* *([Learn how and when to remove this message](/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))* |

Some of the most notable implementations of the idea have been:

- **Baldwin and Gramlich**, as cited above.
- **[eCRUSH](/wiki/ECRUSH "ECRUSH")**. launched Valentine's Day, 1999, is the most successful implementation of the concept. Targeted to the teen market, it has more than 1.6 million users and claims more than 600,000 legitimate matches [[1]](http://www.ecrush.com/faq.phtml?sess_sid=&cobrand=)
- **DoYOU2.com**. The website's owner, [DoYouDo, Inc.](/wiki/DoYouDo "DoYouDo"), was incorporated 23 September 1999 and acquired by [MatchNet](/w/index.php?title=MatchNet&action=edit&redlink=1 "MatchNet (page does not exist)") in September 2000 in exchange for stock valued at $1,820,000. According to MatchNet's 2003 annual report, "The acquisition was made primarily for the purpose of acquiring the patent on this business model for future development."

title: Anonymous matching
text: - **The LiveJournal Secret Crush meme**. In mid-2003, a company named Anonymous Consulting created an online quiz called "Secret Crush Meme,"[[2]](https://web.archive.org/web/20051026032929/http://euthanize.us/memes/secret-crush-meme/) which would provide each user with a chart showing who on their LiveJournal friends list had a crush on them, as well as what "kind" of crush they had (public, secret or ex). The quiz was designed to harvest crushes between [LiveJournal](/wiki/LiveJournal "LiveJournal") users (hence the elaborate disclaimer). In October 2003, a new quiz, called "Secret Crush Meme 2: The Revenge of Secret Crush Meme," was released [[3]](https://web.archive.org/web/20051026025856/http://www.euthanize.us/memes/crushmeme/), which showed users how many crushes other users had on them, as well as what kind. There was a catch: For four dollars, the company would tell someone who had crushes on them. This created controversy between couples who listed other users as crushes as well as people getting ex-crushes when they felt they should have gotten public crushes, and much ethics debating. Finally a small PERL script was written and distributed to poison the database. Faced with attempts to poison the database from many different IP addresses, the project was shut down.

title: Anonymous matching
text:
- **SecretAdmirer.com**. This service claims 100,000 successful matches [[4]](https://web.archive.org/web/20051001034946/http://www.secretadmirer.com/). Salon.com called SecretAdmirer.com "the grandfather of the concept, launched in 1997." [[5]](https://web.archive.org/web/20110606185121/http://dir.salon.com/story/tech/feature/2002/08/07/crushmaster/print.html?pn=2) Its methodology is different from the others in that in order for a match to occur, the recipient must send emails out, rather than simply place names on a confidential list.

These commercial implementations all trust the central server, simplifying the solution and implementation drastically. Baldwin and Gramlich solved this case in 1985, as well as the more notable and challenging case in which the central server isn't trusted.

title: Anonymous matching
text:
## Viral marketing

eCRUSH, DoYOU2.com, the [LiveJournal](/wiki/LiveJournal "LiveJournal") Secret Crush meme, and SecretAdmirer.com are examples of anonymous matching services using [viral marketing](/wiki/Viral_marketing "Viral marketing") to increase their membership. Users are encouraged to send an anonymous email to their crush so that they will visit the site and enter their own crushes, facilitating a match. In the case of SecretAdmirer.com, the email is mandatory; this represents a more aggressive type of viral marketing.

At least one site, CrushLink, was accused by eCRUSH of sending spam emails disguised as crush notifications. According to a [Salon](/wiki/Salon.com "Salon.com") article, "What makes SomeoneLikesYou and Crushlink different from the rest of the sites in the genre is this: they bait hopeful visitors to hand over as many e-mail addresses as possible by trading clues for e-mail addresses"[[6]](https://web.archive.org/web/20051027044313/http://www.salon.com/tech/feature/2002/08/07/crushmaster/print.html). Both sites are now defunct.

title: Backdoor (computing)
text:
Method of bypassing authentication or encryption in a computer

A **backdoor** is a typically covert method of bypassing normal [authentication](/wiki/Authentication "Authentication") or encryption in a computer, product, embedded device (e.g. a [home router](/wiki/Home_router "Home router")), or its embodiment (e.g. part of a [cryptosystem](/wiki/Cryptosystem "Cryptosystem"), [algorithm](/wiki/Algorithm "Algorithm"), [chipset](/wiki/Chipset "Chipset"), or even a "homunculus computer"—a tiny computer-within-a-computer such as that found in Intel's [AMT technology](/wiki/Intel_Active_Management_Technology "Intel Active Management Technology")).[[1]](#cite_note-Eckersley-2017-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Hoffman-2017-2) Backdoors are most often used for securing remote access to a computer, or obtaining access to [plaintext](/wiki/Plaintext "Plaintext") in cryptosystems. From there it may be used to gain access to privileged information like passwords, corrupt or delete data on hard drives, or transfer information within compromised networks.

In the United States, the 1994 [Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act](/wiki/Communications_Assistance_for_Law_Enforcement_Act "Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act") forces internet providers to provide backdoors for government authorities.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) In 2024, the U.S. government realized that China had been tapping communications in the U.S. using that infrastructure for months, or perhaps longer;[[5]](#cite_note-5) China recorded presidential candidate campaign office phone calls—including employees of the then-vice president of the nation, and of the candidates themselves.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

title: Backdoor (computing)
text:
In the United States, the 1994 [Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act](/wiki/Communications_Assistance_for_Law_Enforcement_Act "Communications Assistance for Law Enforcement Act") forces internet providers to provide backdoors for government authorities.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) In 2024, the U.S. government realized that China had been tapping communications in the U.S. using that infrastructure for months, or perhaps longer;[[5]](#cite_note-5) China recorded presidential candidate campaign office phone calls—including employees of the then-vice president of the nation, and of the candidates themselves.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

A backdoor may take the form of a hidden part of a program,[[7]](#cite_note-Wysopal-Eng-7) a separate program (e.g. [Back Orifice](/wiki/Back_Orifice "Back Orifice") may subvert the system through a [rootkit](/wiki/Rootkit "Rootkit")), [code in the firmware](/wiki/Hardware_backdoor "Hardware backdoor") of the hardware,[[8]](#cite_note-Zetter-2013-8) or parts of an [operating system](/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system") such as [Windows](/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows"), for example, [device drivers](/wiki/Device_drivers "Device drivers").[[9]](#cite_note-Ashok-2017-9)[[10]](#cite_note-Microsoft-Back-Doors-10)[[11]](#cite_note-Ars-Technica-2017-11) [Trojan horses](/wiki/Trojan_horse_(computing) "Trojan horse (computing)") can be used to create vulnerabilities in a device. A Trojan horse may appear to be an entirely legitimate program, but when executed, it triggers an activity that may install a backdoor.[[12]](#cite_note-Backdoors-and-Trojan-Horses-12) Although some are secretly installed, other backdoors are deliberate and widely known. These kinds of backdoors have "legitimate" uses such as providing the manufacturer with a way to restore user passwords.

Many systems that store information within the cloud fail to create accurate security measures. If many systems are connected within the [cloud](/wiki/Cloud_computing "Cloud computing"), hackers can gain access to all other platforms through the most vulnerable system.[[13]](#cite_note-Linthicum-13) [Default passwords](/wiki/Default_password "Default password") (or other default credentials) can function as backdoors if they are not changed by the user. Some [debugging](/wiki/Debugging "Debugging") features can also act as backdoors if they are not removed in the release version.[[14]](#cite_note-Bogus-story-14) In 1993, the United States government attempted to deploy an [encryption](/wiki/Encryption "Encryption") system, the [Clipper chip](/wiki/Clipper_chip "Clipper chip"), with an explicit backdoor for law enforcement and national security access. The chip was unsuccessful.[[15]](#cite_note-Clipper-a-failure-15)

Recent proposals to counter backdoors include creating a database of backdoors' triggers and then using [neural networks](/wiki/Neural_network_(machine_learning) "Neural network (machine learning)") to detect them.[[16]](#cite_note-Menisov-2022-16)

title: Backdoor (computing)
text:
## Overview

The threat of backdoors surfaced when multiuser and networked [operating systems](/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system") became widely adopted. Petersen and Turn discussed computer subversion in a paper published in the proceedings of the 1967 AFIPS Conference.[[17]](#cite_note-Petersen-1967-17) They noted a class of active infiltration attacks that use "trapdoor" entry points into the system to bypass security facilities and permit direct access to data. The use of the word *trapdoor* here clearly coincides with more recent definitions of a backdoor. However, since the advent of [public key cryptography](/wiki/Public_key_cryptography "Public key cryptography") the term *trapdoor* has acquired a different meaning (see: [Trapdoor function](/wiki/Trapdoor_function "Trapdoor function")), and thus the term "backdoor" is now preferred, only after the term trapdoor went out of use. More generally, such security breaches were discussed at length in a [RAND Corporation](/wiki/RAND_Corporation "RAND Corporation") task force report published under [DARPA](/wiki/DARPA "DARPA") sponsorship by J.P. Anderson and D.J. Edwards in 1970.[[18]](#cite_note-Security-Controls-18)

While initially targeting the computer vision domain, backdoor attacks have expanded to encompass various other domains, including text, audio, ML-based computer-aided design, and ML-based wireless signal classification. Additionally, vulnerabilities in backdoors have been demonstrated in deep [generative models](/wiki/Generative_model "Generative model"), [reinforcement learning](/wiki/Reinforcement_learning "Reinforcement learning") (e.g., AI GO), and deep graph models. These broad-ranging potential risks have prompted concerns from national security agencies regarding their potentially disastrous consequences.[[19]](#cite_note-19)

Additionally, vulnerabilities in backdoors have been demonstrated in deep [generative models](/wiki/Generative_model "Generative model"), [reinforcement learning](/wiki/Reinforcement_learning "Reinforcement learning") (e.g., AI GO), and deep graph models. These broad-ranging potential risks have prompted concerns from national security agencies regarding their potentially disastrous consequences.[[19]](#cite_note-19)

A backdoor in a login system might take the form of a [hard coded](/wiki/Hard_code "Hard code") user and password combination which gives access to the system. An example of this sort of backdoor was used as a plot device in the [1983](/wiki/1983_in_film "1983 in film") film *[WarGames](/wiki/WarGames "WarGames")*, in which the architect of the "[WOPR](/wiki/WOPR "WOPR")" computer system had inserted a hardcoded password-less account which gave the user access to the system, and to undocumented parts of the system (in particular, a video game-like simulation mode and direct interaction with the [artificial intelligence](/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence")).

Although the number of backdoors in systems using [proprietary software](/wiki/Proprietary_software "Proprietary software") (software whose [source code](/wiki/Source_code "Source code") is not publicly available) is not widely credited, they are nevertheless frequently exposed. Programmers have even succeeded in secretly installing large amounts of benign code as [Easter eggs](/wiki/Easter_egg_(virtual) "Easter egg (virtual)") in programs, although such cases may involve official forbearance, if not actual permission.

title: Backdoor (computing)
text: ## Examples

title: Backdoor (computing)
text:
### Worms

Many [computer worms](/wiki/Computer_worm "Computer worm"), such as [Sobig](/wiki/Sobig "Sobig") and [Mydoom](/wiki/Mydoom "Mydoom"), install a backdoor on the affected computer (generally a [PC](/wiki/IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible") on [broadband](/wiki/Broadband "Broadband") running [Microsoft Windows](/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") and [Microsoft Outlook](/wiki/Microsoft_Outlook "Microsoft Outlook")). Such backdoors appear to be installed so that [spammers](/wiki/E-mail_spam "E-mail spam") can send junk [e-mail](/wiki/Electronic_mail "Electronic mail") from the infected machines. Others, such as the [Sony/BMG rootkit](/wiki/Sony_BMG_CD_copy_prevention_scandal "Sony BMG CD copy prevention scandal"), placed secretly on millions of music CDs through late 2005, are intended as [DRM](/wiki/Digital_rights_management "Digital rights management") measures—and, in that case, as data-gathering [agents](/wiki/Software_agent "Software agent"), since both surreptitious programs they installed routinely contacted central servers.

A sophisticated attempt to plant a backdoor in the [Linux kernel](/wiki/Linux_kernel "Linux kernel"), exposed in November 2003, added a small and subtle code change by subverting the [revision control system](/wiki/Revision_control_system "Revision control system").[[20]](#cite_note-McVoy-20) In this case, a two-line change appeared to *check* [root access](/wiki/Superuser "Superuser") permissions of a caller to the `sys_wait4` function, but because it used assignment `=` instead of equality checking `==`, it actually *granted* permissions to the system. This difference is easily overlooked, and could even be interpreted as an accidental typographical error, rather than an intentional attack.[[21]](#cite_note-An-attempt-to-backdoor-21)[[22]](#cite_note-Poulsen-2003-22)

In January 2014, a backdoor was discovered in certain [Samsung](/wiki/Samsung "Samsung") [Android](/wiki/Android_(operating_system) "Android (operating system)") products, like the Galaxy devices. The Samsung proprietary Android versions are fitted with a backdoor that provides remote access to the data stored on the device. In particular, the Samsung Android software that is in charge of handling the communications with the modem, using the Samsung IPC protocol, implements a class of requests known as remote file server (RFS) commands, that allows the backdoor operator to perform via modem remote I/O operations on the device hard disk or other storage. As the modem is running Samsung proprietary Android software, it is likely that it offers over-the-air remote control that could then be used to issue the RFS commands and thus to access the file system on the device.[[23]](#cite_note-SamsungGalaxyBackdoor-23)

title: Backdoor (computing)
text:
### Object code backdoors

Harder to detect backdoors involve modifying [object code](/wiki/Object_code "Object code"), rather than source code—object code is much harder to inspect, as it is designed to be machine-readable, not human-readable. These backdoors can be inserted either directly in the on-disk object code, or inserted at some point during compilation, assembly linking, or loading—in the latter case the backdoor never appears on disk, only in memory. Object code backdoors are difficult to detect by inspection of the object code, but are easily detected by simply checking for changes (differences), notably in length or in checksum, and in some cases can be detected or analyzed by disassembling the object code. Further, object code backdoors can be removed (assuming source code is available) by simply recompiling from source on a trusted system.

title: Backdoor (computing)
text:
Harder to detect backdoors involve modifying [object code](/wiki/Object_code "Object code"), rather than source code—object code is much harder to inspect, as it is designed to be machine-readable, not human-readable. These backdoors can be inserted either directly in the on-disk object code, or inserted at some point during compilation, assembly linking, or loading—in the latter case the backdoor never appears on disk, only in memory. Object code backdoors are difficult to detect by inspection of the object code, but are easily detected by simply checking for changes (differences), notably in length or in checksum, and in some cases can be detected or analyzed by disassembling the object code. Further, object code backdoors can be removed (assuming source code is available) by simply recompiling from source on a trusted system.

Thus for such backdoors to avoid detection, all extant copies of a binary must be subverted, and any validation checksums must also be compromised, and source must be unavailable, to prevent recompilation. Alternatively, these other tools (length checks, diff, checksumming, disassemblers) can themselves be compromised to conceal the backdoor, for example detecting that the subverted binary is being checksummed and returning the expected value, not the actual value. To conceal these further subversions, the tools must also conceal the changes in themselves—for example, a subverted checksummer must also detect if it is checksumming itself (or other subverted tools) and return false values. This leads to extensive changes in the system and tools being needed to conceal a single change.

Alternatively, these other tools (length checks, diff, checksumming, disassemblers) can themselves be compromised to conceal the backdoor, for example detecting that the subverted binary is being checksummed and returning the expected value, not the actual value. To conceal these further subversions, the tools must also conceal the changes in themselves—for example, a subverted checksummer must also detect if it is checksumming itself (or other subverted tools) and return false values. This leads to extensive changes in the system and tools being needed to conceal a single change.

As object code can be regenerated by recompiling (reassembling, relinking) the original source code, making a persistent object code backdoor (without modifying source code) requires subverting the [compiler](/wiki/Compiler "Compiler") itself—so that when it detects that it is compiling the program under attack it inserts the backdoor—or alternatively the assembler, linker, or loader. As this requires subverting the compiler, this in turn can be fixed by recompiling the compiler, removing the backdoor insertion code. This defense can in turn be subverted by putting a source meta-backdoor in the compiler, so that when it detects that it is compiling itself it then inserts this meta-backdoor generator, together with the original backdoor generator for the original program under attack. After this is done, the source meta-backdoor can be removed, and the compiler recompiled from original source with the compromised compiler executable: the backdoor has been bootstrapped. This attack dates to a 1974 paper by Karger and Schell,[[24]](#cite_note-Karger-Schell-1974-24) and was popularized in Thompson's 1984 article, entitled "Reflections on Trusting Trust";[[25]](#cite_note-Thompson-1984-25) it is hence colloquially known as the "Trusting Trust" attack (see: [§ Compiler backdoors](#Compiler_backdoors), below, for details).

Analogous attacks can target lower levels of the system,
such as the operating system, and can be inserted during the system [booting](/wiki/Booting "Booting") process; these are also mentioned by Karger and Schell in 1974, and now exist in the form of [boot sector viruses](/wiki/Boot_sector_virus "Boot sector virus").[[24]](#cite_note-Karger-Schell-1974-24)[[26]](#cite_note-Karger-Schell-2002-26)

title: Backdoor (computing)
text:
### Asymmetric backdoors

A traditional backdoor is a symmetric backdoor: anyone that finds the backdoor can in turn use it. The notion of an asymmetric backdoor was introduced by Adam Young and [Moti Yung](/wiki/Moti_Yung "Moti Yung") in the *Proceedings of Advances in Cryptology – Crypto '96*. An asymmetric backdoor can only be used by the attacker who plants it, even if the full implementation of the backdoor becomes public (e.g. via publishing, being discovered and disclosed by [reverse engineering](/wiki/Reverse_engineering "Reverse engineering"), etc.). Also, it is computationally intractable to detect the presence of an asymmetric backdoor under black-box queries. This class of attacks have been termed [kleptography](/wiki/Kleptography "Kleptography"); they can be carried out in software, hardware (for example, [smartcards](/wiki/Smartcard "Smartcard")), or a combination of the two. The theory of asymmetric backdoors is part of a larger field now called [cryptovirology](/wiki/Cryptovirology "Cryptovirology"). Notably, [NSA](/wiki/NSA "NSA") inserted a kleptographic backdoor into the [Dual EC DRBG](/wiki/Dual_EC_DRBG "Dual EC DRBG") standard.[[8]](#cite_note-Zetter-2013-8)[[27]](#cite_note-Akkad-2014-27)[[28]](#cite_note-Perlroth-2013-28)

There exists an experimental asymmetric backdoor in [RSA](/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem) "RSA (cryptosystem)") [key](/wiki/Key_(cryptography) "Key (cryptography)") generation. This OpenSSL RSA backdoor, designed by Young and Yung, utilizes a twisted pair of elliptic curves, and has been made available.[[29]](#cite_note-Malicious-Cryptography-29)

title: Backdoor (computing)
section: Backdooring large language models through model poisoning
heading_path: Backdooring large language models through model poisoning
text:
### Backdooring large language models through model poisoning

Model-poisoning in [large language models](/wiki/Large_language_model "Large language model") involves introducing malicious data during the training or [fine-tuning](/wiki/Fine-tuning_(machine_learning) "Fine-tuning (machine learning)") process so that the model behaves normally with standard inputs but activates malicious behavior when a specific backdoor trigger appears. A recent study introduced three attacks—SIMPLE, COVERT, and TROJANPUZZLE—which primarily focus on poisoning [code-generation](/wiki/Source_code "Source code") models by embedding multi-token payloads or out-of-context triggers.[[30]](#cite_note-TrojanPuzzle-2024-30) These attacks demonstrate how even large foundational models can be exploited with subtle poisoning that remains hidden until the specific trigger condition is met.

Since these backdoor attacks target the training pipeline, they evade many traditional defenses that focus on adversarial examples during inference. For example, COVERT and TROJANPUZZLE show how a poisoned sample in a fine-tuning dataset can bypass [static analysis](/wiki/Static_program_analysis "Static program analysis") while remaining undetected by normal validation procedures.[[30]](#cite_note-TrojanPuzzle-2024-30) With open-source or [crowd-sourced datasets](/wiki/Crowdsourcing "Crowdsourcing"), the risk is even higher, since malicious contributions can slip into the update pipeline without a trusted central review process. This makes it difficult for developers to detect the attack until the trigger is activated, often long after the model has been deployed.

Since these backdoor attacks target the training pipeline, they evade many traditional defenses that focus on adversarial examples during inference. For example, COVERT and TROJANPUZZLE show how a poisoned sample in a fine-tuning dataset can bypass [static analysis](/wiki/Static_program_analysis "Static program analysis") while remaining undetected by normal validation procedures.[[30]](#cite_note-TrojanPuzzle-2024-30) With open-source or [crowd-sourced datasets](/wiki/Crowdsourcing "Crowdsourcing"), the risk is even higher, since malicious contributions can slip into the update pipeline without a trusted central review process. This makes it difficult for developers to detect the attack until the trigger is activated, often long after the model has been deployed.

The implications of back-dooring large language models are significant in areas such as [code generation](/wiki/Source_code "Source code") or the potential leaking of sensitive information when specific triggers are activated. Researchers have shown how [model poisoning](/wiki/Data_poisoning "Data poisoning") can manipulate the behavior of models trained on massive datasets while maintaining high performance on benign inputs.[[30]](#cite_note-TrojanPuzzle-2024-30) These risks highlight the need for more rigorous dataset auditing, trigger testing, and continuous monitoring of model outputs across different contexts.

title: Backdoor (computing)
heading_path: Backdooring large language models through model poisoning
text:
#### Latent-space backdoors in malware detection

Recent research has found that some deep learning based [malware](/wiki/Malware "Malware") detectors can be attacked using latent space backdoors, a kind of training time [data poisoning](/wiki/Data_poisoning "Data poisoning") attack where the trigger is hidden inside the model's internal features instead of appearing as a fixed pattern in the input bytes. Unlike traditional backdoors or [Trojans](/wiki/Trojan_horse_(computing) "Trojan horse (computing)") that usually depend on specific byte sequences added to an executable, latent space backdoors work at a more semantic level, where many different byte patterns can be turned by the model's [embedding](/wiki/Embedding "Embedding") and [pooling layers](/wiki/Pooling_layer "Pooling layer") into a similar hidden representation. This means the trigger is not tied to one exact substring in the binary and can still work even if the input has been changed to remove simple noise.

text:
Recent research has found that some deep learning based [malware](/wiki/Malware "Malware") detectors can be attacked using latent space backdoors, a kind of training time [data poisoning](/wiki/Data_poisoning "Data poisoning") attack where the trigger is hidden inside the model's internal features instead of appearing as a fixed pattern in the input bytes. Unlike traditional backdoors or [Trojans](/wiki/Trojan_horse_(computing) "Trojan horse (computing)") that usually depend on specific byte sequences added to an executable, latent space backdoors work at a more semantic level, where many different byte patterns can be turned by the model's [embedding](/wiki/Embedding "Embedding") and [pooling layers](/wiki/Pooling_layer "Pooling layer") into a similar hidden representation. This means the trigger is not tied to one exact substring in the binary and can still work even if the input has been changed to remove simple noise.

These attacks are especially important for deep learning based malware classifiers such as MalConv, where [convolutional](/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network "Convolutional neural network") and pooling operations remove small local irregularities in the bytes but keep higher level learned features. An attacker can poison a very small part of the training data, sometimes reported as less than 0.1%, and still cause the model to learn an internal rule that treats any file that matches a certain hidden pattern as harmless, even when the visible bytes look quite different across samples. Because the model can still perform well on clean validation data, these backdoors can slip through normal testing and stay active when the system is deployed in practice.

These attacks are especially important for deep learning based malware classifiers such as MalConv, where [convolutional](/wiki/Convolutional_neural_network "Convolutional neural network") and pooling operations remove small local irregularities in the bytes but keep higher level learned features. An attacker can poison a very small part of the training data, sometimes reported as less than 0.1%, and still cause the model to learn an internal rule that treats any file that matches a certain hidden pattern as harmless, even when the visible bytes look quite different across samples. Because the model can still perform well on clean validation data, these backdoors can slip through normal testing and stay active when the system is deployed in practice.

Defending against latent space backdoors is harder than dealing with attacks that use a simple, static trigger. Many defenses focus on changing the input slightly or using separate neural networks to spot Trojans, and they often assume that small changes to the input will break the trigger or that backdoors always line up with simple feature patterns. In latent space attacks, changing the raw bytes may leave the important internal activation pattern almost untouched, and detectors trained on basic backdoor examples may not see the more spread out correlations that these attacks rely on. This has led researchers to explore defenses that pay closer attention to internal representations, keep better track of how training data is collected and cleaned, and monitor neural activations over time instead of only looking at the input bytes.[[31]](#cite_note-BackdoorMalware-31)

title: Backdoor (computing)
text:
## Compiler backdoors

A sophisticated form of [black box](/wiki/Black_box "Black box") backdoor is a **compiler backdoor**, where not only is a compiler subverted—to insert a backdoor in some other program, such as a login program—but it is further modified to detect when it is compiling itself and then inserts both the backdoor insertion code (targeting the other program) and the code-modifying self-compilation, like the mechanism through which [retroviruses](/wiki/Retrovirus "Retrovirus") infect their host. This can be done by modifying the source code, and the resulting compromised compiler (object code) can compile the original (unmodified) source code and insert itself: the exploit has been boot-strapped.

This attack was originally presented in Karger & Schell (1974),[[note 1]](#cite_note-32) which was a [United States Air Force](/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") security analysis of [Multics](/wiki/Multics "Multics"), where they described such an attack on a [PL/I](/wiki/PL/I "PL/I") compiler, and call it a "compiler trap door". They also mention a variant where the system initialization code is modified to insert a backdoor during [booting](/wiki/Booting "Booting"), as this is complex and poorly understood, and call it an "initialization trapdoor"; this is now known as a [boot sector virus](/wiki/Boot_sector_virus "Boot sector virus").[[26]](#cite_note-Karger-Schell-2002-26)

title: Backdoor (computing)
text:
This attack was originally presented in Karger & Schell (1974),[[note 1]](#cite_note-32) which was a [United States Air Force](/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") security analysis of [Multics](/wiki/Multics "Multics"), where they described such an attack on a [PL/I](/wiki/PL/I "PL/I") compiler, and call it a "compiler trap door". They also mention a variant where the system initialization code is modified to insert a backdoor during [booting](/wiki/Booting "Booting"), as this is complex and poorly understood, and call it an "initialization trapdoor"; this is now known as a [boot sector virus](/wiki/Boot_sector_virus "Boot sector virus").[[26]](#cite_note-Karger-Schell-2002-26)

This attack was then actually implemented by [Ken Thompson](/wiki/Ken_Thompson "Ken Thompson"), and popularized in his [Turing Award](/wiki/Turing_Award "Turing Award") acceptance speech in 1983, "Reflections on Trusting Trust",[[25]](#cite_note-Thompson-1984-25) which points out that trust is relative, and the only software one can truly trust is code where every step of the bootstrapping has been inspected. This backdoor mechanism is based on the fact that people only review source (human-written) code, and not compiled [machine code](/wiki/Machine_code "Machine code") ([object code](/wiki/Object_code "Object code")). A [program](/wiki/Software "Software") called a [compiler](/wiki/Compiler "Compiler") is used to create the second from the first, and the compiler is usually trusted to do an honest job.

title: Backdoor (computing)
text:
This attack was then actually implemented by [Ken Thompson](/wiki/Ken_Thompson "Ken Thompson"), and popularized in his [Turing Award](/wiki/Turing_Award "Turing Award") acceptance speech in 1983, "Reflections on Trusting Trust",[[25]](#cite_note-Thompson-1984-25) which points out that trust is relative, and the only software one can truly trust is code where every step of the bootstrapping has been inspected. This backdoor mechanism is based on the fact that people only review source (human-written) code, and not compiled [machine code](/wiki/Machine_code "Machine code") ([object code](/wiki/Object_code "Object code")). A [program](/wiki/Software "Software") called a [compiler](/wiki/Compiler "Compiler") is used to create the second from the first, and the compiler is usually trusted to do an honest job.

Thompson's paper[[25]](#cite_note-Thompson-1984-25) describes a modified version of the [Unix](/wiki/Unix "Unix") [C](/wiki/C_(programming_language) "C (programming language)") compiler that would put an invisible backdoor in the Unix [login](/wiki/Logging_(computer_security) "Logging (computer security)") command when it noticed that the login program was being compiled, and would also add this feature undetectably to future compiler versions upon their compilation as well. As the compiler itself was a compiled program, users would be extremely unlikely to notice the machine code instructions that performed these tasks. (Because of the second task, the compiler's source code would appear "clean".) What's worse, in Thompson's [proof of concept](/wiki/Proof_of_concept "Proof of concept") implementation, the subverted compiler also subverted the analysis program (the [disassembler](/wiki/Disassembler "Disassembler")), so that anyone who examined the binaries in the usual way would not actually see the real code that was running, but something else instead.

As the compiler itself was a compiled program, users would be extremely unlikely to notice the machine code instructions that performed these tasks. (Because of the second task, the compiler's source code would appear "clean".) What's worse, in Thompson's [proof of concept](/wiki/Proof_of_concept "Proof of concept") implementation, the subverted compiler also subverted the analysis program (the [disassembler](/wiki/Disassembler "Disassembler")), so that anyone who examined the binaries in the usual way would not actually see the real code that was running, but something else instead.

Karger and Schell gave an updated analysis of the original exploit in 2002, and, in 2009, Wheeler wrote a historical overview and survey of the literature.[[note 2]](#cite_note-34) In 2023, Cox published an annotated version of Thompson's backdoor source code.[[33]](#cite_note-35)

title: Backdoor (computing)
text:
### Occurrences

Thompson's version was, officially, never released into the wild. However, it is believed that a version was distributed to [BBN](/wiki/BBN_Technologies "BBN Technologies") and at least one use of the backdoor was recorded.[[note 3]](#cite_note-37) There are scattered anecdotal reports of such backdoors in subsequent years.

In August 2009, an attack of this kind was discovered by Sophos labs. The W32/Induc-A virus infected the program compiler for [Delphi](/wiki/Delphi_(programming_language) "Delphi (programming language)"), a Windows programming language. The virus introduced its own code to the compilation of new Delphi programs, allowing it to infect and propagate to many systems, without the knowledge of the software programmer. The virus looks for a Delphi installation, modifies the SysConst.pas file, which is the source code of a part of the standard library and compiles it. After that, every program compiled by that Delphi installation will contain the virus. An attack that propagates by building its own [Trojan horse](/wiki/Trojan_horse_(computing) "Trojan horse (computing)") can be especially hard to discover. It resulted in many software vendors releasing infected executables without realizing it, sometimes claiming false positives. After all, the executable was not tampered with, the compiler was. It is believed that the Induc-A virus had been propagating for at least a year before it was discovered.[[note 4]](#cite_note-39)

title: Backdoor (computing)
text:
In August 2009, an attack of this kind was discovered by Sophos labs. The W32/Induc-A virus infected the program compiler for [Delphi](/wiki/Delphi_(programming_language) "Delphi (programming language)"), a Windows programming language. The virus introduced its own code to the compilation of new Delphi programs, allowing it to infect and propagate to many systems, without the knowledge of the software programmer. The virus looks for a Delphi installation, modifies the SysConst.pas file, which is the source code of a part of the standard library and compiles it. After that, every program compiled by that Delphi installation will contain the virus. An attack that propagates by building its own [Trojan horse](/wiki/Trojan_horse_(computing) "Trojan horse (computing)") can be especially hard to discover. It resulted in many software vendors releasing infected executables without realizing it, sometimes claiming false positives. After all, the executable was not tampered with, the compiler was. It is believed that the Induc-A virus had been propagating for at least a year before it was discovered.[[note 4]](#cite_note-39)

In 2015, a malicious copy of Xcode, [XcodeGhost](/wiki/XcodeGhost "XcodeGhost"), also performed a similar attack and infected iOS apps from a dozen of software companies in China. Globally, 4,000 apps were found to be affected. It was not a true Thompson Trojan, as it does not infect development tools themselves, but it did prove that toolchain poisoning can cause substantial damages.[[36]](#cite_note-XcodeGhost-40)

title: Backdoor (computing)
text:
### Countermeasures

Once a system has been compromised with a backdoor or Trojan horse, such as the *Trusting Trust* compiler, it is very hard for the "rightful" user to regain control of the system – typically one should rebuild a clean system and transfer data (but not executables) over. However, several practical weaknesses in the *Trusting Trust* scheme have been suggested. For example, a sufficiently motivated user could painstakingly review the machine code of the untrusted compiler before using it. As mentioned above, there are ways to hide the Trojan horse, such as subverting the disassembler; but there are ways to counter that defense, too, such as writing a disassembler from scratch.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

title: Backdoor (computing)
text:
Once a system has been compromised with a backdoor or Trojan horse, such as the *Trusting Trust* compiler, it is very hard for the "rightful" user to regain control of the system – typically one should rebuild a clean system and transfer data (but not executables) over. However, several practical weaknesses in the *Trusting Trust* scheme have been suggested. For example, a sufficiently motivated user could painstakingly review the machine code of the untrusted compiler before using it. As mentioned above, there are ways to hide the Trojan horse, such as subverting the disassembler; but there are ways to counter that defense, too, such as writing a disassembler from scratch.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

A generic method to counter trusting trust attacks is called **diverse double-compiling**. The method requires a different compiler and the source code of the compiler-under-test. That source, compiled with both compilers, results in two different stage-1 compilers, which however should have the same behavior. Thus the same source compiled with both stage-1 compilers must then result in two identical stage-2 compilers. A formal proof is given that the latter comparison guarantees that the purported source code and executable of the compiler-under-test correspond, under some assumptions. This method was applied by its author to verify that the C compiler of the [GCC suite](/wiki/GNU_Compiler_Collection "GNU Compiler Collection") (v. 3.0.4) contained no trojan, using [icc](/wiki/Intel_C%2B%2B_Compiler "Intel C++ Compiler") (v. 11.0) as the different compiler.[[32]](#cite_note-Wheeler-2009-33)

title: Backdoor (computing)
text:
A generic method to counter trusting trust attacks is called **diverse double-compiling**. The method requires a different compiler and the source code of the compiler-under-test. That source, compiled with both compilers, results in two different stage-1 compilers, which however should have the same behavior. Thus the same source compiled with both stage-1 compilers must then result in two identical stage-2 compilers. A formal proof is given that the latter comparison guarantees that the purported source code and executable of the compiler-under-test correspond, under some assumptions. This method was applied by its author to verify that the C compiler of the [GCC suite](/wiki/GNU_Compiler_Collection "GNU Compiler Collection") (v. 3.0.4) contained no trojan, using [icc](/wiki/Intel_C%2B%2B_Compiler "Intel C++ Compiler") (v. 11.0) as the different compiler.[[32]](#cite_note-Wheeler-2009-33)

In practice such verifications are not done by end users, except in extreme circumstances of intrusion detection and analysis, due to the rarity of such sophisticated attacks, and because programs are typically distributed in binary form. Removing backdoors (including compiler backdoors) is typically done by simply rebuilding a clean system. However, the sophisticated verifications are of interest to operating system vendors, to ensure that they are not distributing a compromised system, and in high-security settings, where such attacks are a realistic concern.

title: Backdoor (computing)
text:
## List of known backdoors

- [Back Orifice](/wiki/Back_Orifice "Back Orifice") was created in 1998 by [hackers](/wiki/Hacker_(computer_security) "Hacker (computer security)") from [Cult of the Dead Cow](/wiki/Cult_of_the_Dead_Cow "Cult of the Dead Cow") group as a remote administration tool. It allowed [Windows](/wiki/Windows "Windows") computers to be remotely controlled over a network and parodied the name of Microsoft's [BackOffice](/wiki/BackOffice "BackOffice").
- The [Dual EC DRBG](/wiki/Dual_EC_DRBG "Dual EC DRBG") [cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator](/wiki/Cryptographically_secure_pseudorandom_number_generator "Cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator") was revealed in 2013 to possibly have a [kleptographic](/wiki/Kleptography "Kleptography") backdoor deliberately inserted by NSA, who also had the private key to the backdoor.[[8]](#cite_note-Zetter-2013-8)[[28]](#cite_note-Perlroth-2013-28)
- Several backdoors in the [unlicensed](/wiki/Copyright_infringement "Copyright infringement") copies of [WordPress](/wiki/WordPress "WordPress") [plug-ins](/wiki/Plug-in_(computing) "Plug-in (computing)") were discovered in March 2014.[[37]](#cite_note-WordPress-41) They were inserted as [obfuscated](/wiki/Obfuscation_(software) "Obfuscation (software)") [JavaScript](/wiki/JavaScript "JavaScript") code and silently created, for example, an [admin](/wiki/System_administrator "System administrator") account in the website database. A similar scheme was later exposed in a [Joomla](/wiki/Joomla "Joomla") plugin.[[38]](#cite_note-Sinegubko-2014-42)

title: Backdoor (computing)
text:
- [Borland](/wiki/Borland "Borland") [Interbase](/wiki/Interbase "Interbase") versions 4.0 through 6.0 had a hard-coded backdoor, put there by the developers. The server code contains a compiled-in backdoor account (username: *politically*, password: *correct*), which could be accessed over a network connection; a user logging in with this backdoor account could take full control over all Interbase databases. The backdoor was detected in 2001 and a [patch](/wiki/Patch_(computing) "Patch (computing)") was released.[[39]](#cite_note-Vulnerability-43)[[40]](#cite_note-Interbase-Server-44)
- [Juniper Networks](/wiki/Juniper_Networks "Juniper Networks") backdoor inserted in the year 2008 into the versions of firmware [ScreenOS](/wiki/ScreenOS "ScreenOS") from 6.2.0r15 to 6.2.0r18 and from 6.3.0r12 to 6.3.0r20[[41]](#cite_note-Juniper-firewall-45) that gives any user administrative access when using a special master password.[[42]](#cite_note-Zagrozenia-46)
- Several backdoors were discovered in C-DATA Optical Line Termination (OLT) devices.[[43]](#cite_note-CDATA-OLTs-47) Researchers released the findings without notifying C-DATA because they believe the backdoors were intentionally placed by the vendor.[[44]](#cite_note-FTTH-devices-48)

title: Backdoor (computing)
text: - A backdoor in versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 of the popular Linux utility [XZ Utils](/wiki/XZ_Utils "XZ Utils") was [discovered in March 2024](/wiki/XZ_Utils_backdoor "XZ Utils backdoor") by software developer Andres Freund.[[45]](#cite_note-register-49) The backdoor gives an attacker who possesses a specific [Ed448](/wiki/Ed448 "Ed448") private key [remote code execution](/wiki/Remote_code_execution "Remote code execution") capabilities on the affected Linux systems. The issue has been assigned a [CVSS](/wiki/Common_Vulnerability_Scoring_System "Common Vulnerability Scoring System") score of 10.0, the highest possible score.[[46]](#cite_note-50)[[47]](#cite_note-51)[[48]](#cite_note-SamJames-52)

title: Batch cryptography
text: **Batch cryptography** is a field of [cryptology](/wiki/Cryptology "Cryptology") focused on the design of [cryptographic protocols](/wiki/Cryptographic_protocol "Cryptographic protocol") that perform operations—such as [encryption](/wiki/Encryption "Encryption"), decryption, [key exchange](/wiki/Key_exchange "Key exchange"), and [authentication](/wiki/Authentication "Authentication")—on multiple inputs simultaneously, rather than processing each input individually.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Batching cryptographic operations can significantly reduce the marginal cost of handling individual inputs—a principle that was first introduced by Amos Fiat in 1989.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

title: Adaptive redaction
text: **Adaptive redaction** is a form of [redaction](/wiki/Redaction "Redaction") whereby sensitive parts of a document are automatically removed based on [policy](/wiki/Policy "Policy")[[1]](#cite_note-1). It is primarily used in next generation [Data Loss Prevention](/wiki/Data_loss_prevention_software "Data loss prevention software") (DLP) solutions.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

title: Adaptive redaction
text:
## Content and context

The policy is a set of rules based on content and context. Context can include:

- Who is sending (or uploading) the information.
- Who is receiving the information (including a website if uploading or downloading).
- The communication channel (e.g. email, web, copy to removable media).

The content can be 'visible' information, such as that you see on the screen. For example, sending unprotected [credit card](/wiki/Credit_card "Credit card") information outside an organisation breaches the [Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard](/wiki/Payment_Card_Industry_Data_Security_Standard "Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard") (PCI DSS regulations). Many organisations accept credit card information through incoming [email](/wiki/Email "Email"), but a reply to an email containing such information would send out the prohibited information. That would cause a breach of policy. Adaptive redaction can therefore be used to remove just the credit card number but allow the email to be sent.

Content can also be 'invisible' information such as that in [document](/wiki/Electronic_document "Electronic document") properties and [revision history](/wiki/Revision_history "Revision history"), and it can also be 'active' content which has been embedded in an electronic document, such as a [macro](/wiki/Macro_(computer_science) "Macro (computer science)"). Release of 'invisible' information has on several occasions created embarrassment for government bodies.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

title: Adaptive redaction
text:
## Purpose

Adaptive redaction is designed to alleviate "False Positive" events created with [Data loss prevention software](/wiki/Data_loss_prevention_software "Data loss prevention software") (DLP) security solutions[[5]](#cite_note-5). False positives occur when a DLP policy triggers and prevents legitimate outgoing communication[[6]](#cite_note-6). In the majority of cases this is caused through oversight by the sender.

title: Blinding (cryptography)
text:
Computing without having input or output

In [cryptography](/wiki/Cryptography "Cryptography"), **blinding** first became known in the context of [blind signatures](/wiki/Blind_signature "Blind signature"), where the message author *blinds* the message with a random *blinding factor*, the signer then signs it and the message author "*unblinds"* it*;* signer and message author are different parties.

Since the late 1990s, **blinding** mostly refers to countermeasures against [side-channel attacks](/wiki/Side-channel_attacks "Side-channel attacks") on encryption devices,[[1]](#cite_note-1) where the random *blinding* and the "*unblinding"* happen on the encryption devices. The techniques used for blinding signatures were adapted to prevent attackers from knowing the input to the [modular exponentiation](/wiki/Modular_exponentiation "Modular exponentiation") function for [Diffie-Hellman](/wiki/Diffie-Hellman "Diffie-Hellman") or [RSA](/wiki/RSA_cryptosystem "RSA cryptosystem").

Blinding must be applied with care, for example [Rabin–Williams signatures](/wiki/Rabin_signature "Rabin signature"). If blinding is applied to the formatted message but the random value does not honor Jacobi requirements on *p* and *q*, then it could lead to private key recovery. A demonstration of the recovery can be seen in [CVE](/wiki/Common_Vulnerabilities_and_Exposures "Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures")-2015-2141[[2]](#cite_note-2) discovered by Evgeny Sidorov.

title: Blinding (cryptography)
text:
Blinding must be applied with care, for example [Rabin–Williams signatures](/wiki/Rabin_signature "Rabin signature"). If blinding is applied to the formatted message but the random value does not honor Jacobi requirements on *p* and *q*, then it could lead to private key recovery. A demonstration of the recovery can be seen in [CVE](/wiki/Common_Vulnerabilities_and_Exposures "Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures")-2015-2141[[2]](#cite_note-2) discovered by Evgeny Sidorov.

Side-channel attacks allow an adversary to recover information about the input to a cryptographic operation within an [asymmetric encryption scheme](/wiki/Asymmetric_key_encryption_algorithm "Asymmetric key encryption algorithm"), by measuring something other than the algorithm's result, e.g., power consumption, computation time, or radio-frequency emanations by a device. Typically these attacks depend on the attacker knowing the characteristics of the algorithm, as well as (some) inputs. In this setting, blinding serves to alter the algorithm's input into some unpredictable state. Depending on the characteristics of the blinding function, this can prevent some or all leakage of useful information. Note that security depends also on the resistance of the blinding functions themselves to side-channel attacks.

title: Blinding (cryptography)
text:
## Examples

- In [RSA](/wiki/RSA_(algorithm) "RSA (algorithm)") blinding involves computing the blinding operation *E*(*x*) = *(xr)e* mod *N*, where *r* is a random integer between 1 and *N* and [relatively prime](/wiki/Relatively_prime "Relatively prime") to *N* (i.e. gcd(*r*, *N*) = 1), *x* is the [plaintext](/wiki/Plaintext "Plaintext"), *e* is the public RSA exponent and *N* is the RSA modulus. As usual, the decryption function *f*(*z*) = *zd* mod *N* is applied thus giving *f*(*E*(*x*)) = *(xr)ed* mod *N* = *xr* mod *N*. Finally it is unblinded using the function *D*(*z*) = *zr*−1 mod *N*. Multiplying *xr* mod *N* by *r−1* mod *N* yields *x*, as desired. When decrypting in this manner, an adversary who is able to measure time taken by this operation would not be able to make use of this information (by applying timing attacks RSA is known to be vulnerable to) as they does not know the constant *r* and hence has no knowledge of the real input fed to the RSA primitives.

- [Blinding in GPG 1.x](http://git.gnupg.org/cgi-bin/gitweb.cgi?p=gnupg.git;a=commit;h=93a96e3c0c33370248f6570d8285c4e811d305d4)

**123 Reg** is a British [domain registrar](/wiki/Domain_name_registrar "Domain name registrar") and [web hosting](/wiki/Web_hosting "Web hosting") company, founded in Britain in 2000 and now under the ultimate ownership of [GoDaddy](/wiki/GoDaddy "GoDaddy"). The company claims to be the UK's largest[[2]](#cite_note-2) accredited[[3]](#cite_note-3) domain registrar and provides Internet services to small- and medium-sized business. From 2003 to 2017, 123 Reg was part of [Host Europe Group](/wiki/Host_Europe_Group "Host Europe Group") (HEG). In April 2017, American hosting company GoDaddy acquired HEG for 1.69 billion euros ($1.82 billion).[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4)

title: 123 Reg
text:
## History

123 Reg was founded in Britain in 2000 by Jonathan and Tim Beresford-Brealey,[[5]](#cite_note-:2-5) who prior to this had also set up Webfusion Internet Solutions Ltd in 1997.[[6]](#cite_note-6) In 2003, 123 Reg and Webfusion were acquired by Host Europe Group (HEG).[[5]](#cite_note-:2-5) In 2004, Host Europe Group was bought by [Pipex Communications](/wiki/Pipex_Communications "Pipex Communications") for £31.2m[[7]](#cite_note-7) and 123 Reg became the UK's largest domain registrar, according to the company's parent.[[8]](#cite_note-:1-8)

title: 123 Reg
text:
123 Reg was founded in Britain in 2000 by Jonathan and Tim Beresford-Brealey,[[5]](#cite_note-:2-5) who prior to this had also set up Webfusion Internet Solutions Ltd in 1997.[[6]](#cite_note-6) In 2003, 123 Reg and Webfusion were acquired by Host Europe Group (HEG).[[5]](#cite_note-:2-5) In 2004, Host Europe Group was bought by [Pipex Communications](/wiki/Pipex_Communications "Pipex Communications") for £31.2m[[7]](#cite_note-7) and 123 Reg became the UK's largest domain registrar, according to the company's parent.[[8]](#cite_note-:1-8)

In 2009, Host Europe Group organised its UK operations under the Webfusion Ltd group but kept both brands.[[8]](#cite_note-:1-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9) The same year, Webfusion became the first UK web host to offer [Windows Server 2008](/wiki/Windows_Server_2008 "Windows Server 2008") web hosting,[[8]](#cite_note-:1-8) and the company opened a £2.5 million data centre in [Leeds](/wiki/Leeds "Leeds").[[10]](#cite_note-10) Also in 2009, 123 Reg became the first UK domain registrar to have 2 million domain names on register.[[8]](#cite_note-:1-8) In 2010, Webfusion Ltd was included on *[The Sunday Times's](/wiki/The_Sunday_Times "The Sunday Times")* list of Britain's fastest-growing private-equity backed companies, the [Deloitte](/wiki/Deloitte "Deloitte") Buyout Track 100, and was the only hosting company on the list.[[11]](#cite_note-11) In 2012, it became the first UK domain registrar to have 3 million domain names on register.[[8]](#cite_note-:1-8)

In 2009, Host Europe Group organised its UK operations under the Webfusion Ltd group but kept both brands.[[8]](#cite_note-:1-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9) The same year, Webfusion became the first UK web host to offer [Windows Server 2008](/wiki/Windows_Server_2008 "Windows Server 2008") web hosting,[[8]](#cite_note-:1-8) and the company opened a £2.5 million data centre in [Leeds](/wiki/Leeds "Leeds").[[10]](#cite_note-10) Also in 2009, 123 Reg became the first UK domain registrar to have 2 million domain names on register.[[8]](#cite_note-:1-8) In 2010, Webfusion Ltd was included on *[The Sunday Times's](/wiki/The_Sunday_Times "The Sunday Times")* list of Britain's fastest-growing private-equity backed companies, the [Deloitte](/wiki/Deloitte "Deloitte") Buyout Track 100, and was the only hosting company on the list.[[11]](#cite_note-11) In 2012, it became the first UK domain registrar to have 3 million domain names on register.[[8]](#cite_note-:1-8)

On 16 April 2016, 123 Reg admitted a major deletion of a large number of [virtual private servers](/wiki/Virtual_private_servers "Virtual private servers") (VPSs) caused by an error during what should have been routine maintenance.[[12]](#cite_note-12) The event deleted hundreds of websites, with users losing sites and access to data on their VPS service. By 24 April, the situation was still ongoing. During this period, 123 Reg had a further [data breach](/wiki/Data_breach "Data breach"), with customers being able to see the support tickets of other account holders.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

A **privacy-focused remailer** is a [server](/wiki/Server_(computing) "Server (computing)") that receives messages with embedded instructions on where to send them next, and that forwards them while attempting to obscure their origin. There are [cypherpunk remailers](/wiki/Cypherpunk_anonymous_remailer "Cypherpunk anonymous remailer"), [mixmaster remailers](/wiki/Mixmaster_anonymous_remailer "Mixmaster anonymous remailer"), and [nym servers](/wiki/Pseudonymous_remailer "Pseudonymous remailer"), among others, which differ in their design and the level of privacy they were intended to provide. It is critical to understand that without integration with an anonymity network like Tor, these systems do not provide anonymity against powerful adversaries.

title: Anonymous remailer
text:
A **privacy-focused remailer** is a [server](/wiki/Server_(computing) "Server (computing)") that receives messages with embedded instructions on where to send them next, and that forwards them while attempting to obscure their origin. There are [cypherpunk remailers](/wiki/Cypherpunk_anonymous_remailer "Cypherpunk anonymous remailer"), [mixmaster remailers](/wiki/Mixmaster_anonymous_remailer "Mixmaster anonymous remailer"), and [nym servers](/wiki/Pseudonymous_remailer "Pseudonymous remailer"), among others, which differ in their design and the level of privacy they were intended to provide. It is critical to understand that without integration with an anonymity network like Tor, these systems do not provide anonymity against powerful adversaries.

*Remailing* as discussed in this article applies to e-mails intended for particular recipients, not the general public. Anonymity in the latter case is more easily addressed by using any of several methods of anonymous publication.
*Remailing* should also not be confused with modern services providing an [email alias](/wiki/Email_alias "Email alias").

title: Anonymous remailer
text:
## Types of remailers

There are several strategies that affect the pseudonymity of the handled e-mail. These classes of remailers differ with regard to the choices their designers/operators have made. These choices can be influenced by the legal ramifications of operating specific types of remailers.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

It must be understood that every [data packet](/wiki/Data_packet "Data packet") traveling on the [Internet](/wiki/Internet "Internet") contains the node addresses (as raw [IP](/wiki/Internet_Protocol "Internet Protocol") bit strings) of both the sending and intended recipient nodes, and so no data packet can *ever* actually be anonymous at this level [*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]. In addition, all standards-based e-mail messages contain defined fields in their headers in which the source and transmitting entities (and Internet nodes as well) are required to be included.

Some remailers change both types of address in messages they forward, and the list of forwarding nodes in e-mail messages as well, as the message passes through; in effect, they substitute 'fake source addresses' for the originals. The 'IP source address' for that packet may become that of the remailer server itself, and within an e-mail message (which is usually several packets), a nominal 'user' on that server. Some remailers forward their anonymized e-mail to still other remailers, and only after several such hops is the e-mail actually delivered to the intended address.

There are, more or less, four types of remailers:

title: Anonymous remailer
text:
### Pseudonymous remailers

A [pseudonymous remailer](/wiki/Pseudonymous_remailer "Pseudonymous remailer") simply takes away the e-mail address of the sender, gives a pseudonym to the sender, and sends the message to the intended recipient (that can be answered via that remailer).[[2]](#cite_note-2)

title: Anonymous remailer
text:
### Cypherpunk remailers

A [Cypherpunk remailer](/wiki/Cypherpunk_anonymous_remailer "Cypherpunk anonymous remailer") sends the message to the recipient, stripping away the sender address on it. One can not answer a message sent via a Cypherpunk remailer. The message sent to the remailer can usually be encrypted, and the remailer will decrypt it and send it to the recipient address hidden inside the encrypted message. In addition, it is possible to chain two or three remailers, so that each remailer can't know who is sending a message to whom. Cypherpunk remailers typically do not keep logs of transactions, but their design is vulnerable to traffic analysis.

title: Anonymous remailer
text:
### Mixmaster remailers

In [Mixmaster](/wiki/Mixmaster_anonymous_remailer "Mixmaster anonymous remailer"), the user composes an email to a remailer, which is relayed through each node in the network using [SMTP](/wiki/SMTP "SMTP"), until it finally arrives at the final recipient. Mixmaster can only send emails one way. An email is sent pseudonymously to an individual, but for them to be able to respond, a reply address must be included in the body of the email. Also, Mixmaster remailers require the use of a [computer program](/wiki/Computer_program "Computer program") to write messages. Such programs are not supplied as a standard part of most operating systems or mail management systems. Mixmaster is vulnerable to long-term traffic analysis and is considered obsolete.

title: Anonymous remailer
text:
### Mixminion remailers

A [Mixminion](/wiki/Mixminion "Mixminion") remailer attempts to address the following challenges in Mixmaster remailers: replies, forward anonymity, replay prevention and key rotation, exit policies, integrated directory servers and dummy traffic. They are currently available for the Linux and Windows platforms. Some implementations are open source. Despite improvements, Mixminion shares the fundamental vulnerability to traffic analysis and requires protection by a network like Tor for meaningful anonymity.

title: Anonymous remailer
text:
## Traceable remailers

Some remailers establish an internal list of actual senders and invented names such that a recipient can send mail to *invented name* AT *some-remailer.example*. When receiving traffic addressed to this user, the server software consults that list, and forwards the mail to the original sender, thus permitting anonymous—though traceable with access to the list—two-way communication. The famous "[penet.fi](/wiki/Penet_remailer "Penet remailer")" remailer in Finland did just that for several years.[[3]](#cite_note-3) Because of the existence of such lists in this type of remailing server, it is possible to break the anonymity by gaining access to the list(s), by breaking into the computer, asking a court (or merely the police in some places) to order that the anonymity be broken, and/or bribing an attendant. This happened to penet.fi as a result of some traffic passed through it about [Scientology](/wiki/Scientology "Scientology").[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] The Church claimed [copyright infringement](/wiki/Copyright_infringement "Copyright infringement") and sued penet.fi's operator. A court ordered the list be made available. Penet's operator shut it down after destroying its records (including the list) to retain [identity](/wiki/Digital_identity "Digital identity") [confidentiality](/wiki/Confidentiality "Confidentiality") for its users; though not before being forced to supply the court with the real e-mail addresses of two of its users.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

A court ordered the list be made available. More recent remailer designs use [cryptography](/wiki/Cryptography "Cryptography") in an attempt to provide more or less the same service, but without so much risk of loss of user confidentiality. These are generally termed [nym servers](/wiki/Nym_server "Nym server") or [pseudonymous remailers](/wiki/Pseudonymous_remailer "Pseudonymous remailer"). The degree to which they remain vulnerable to forced disclosure (by courts or police) is and will remain unclear since new statutes/regulations and new [cryptanalytic](/wiki/Cryptanalytic "Cryptanalytic") developments proceed apace. Multiple anonymous forwarding among cooperating remailers in different jurisdictions may retain, but cannot guarantee, anonymity against a determined attempt by one or more governments, or civil litigators.

title: Anonymous remailer
text:
## Modern Tor-based and Mixnet alternatives

Due to the inherent vulnerabilities of classical remailers to [traffic correlation](/wiki/Traffic_analysis "Traffic analysis")[[4]](#cite_note-Danezis2006-4) and metadata surveillance, the modern approach to anonymous email relies on integrating remailer functionality with robust anonymity networks.

**Tor-based remailers:** Systems like the **Onion Courier Mixnet**[[5]](#cite_note-OnionCourier-5) operate as [Tor](/wiki/Tor_(network) "Tor (network)") hidden services. This protects the user's IP address and the remailer's location from network observers. While Tor provides strong protection for network metadata, the mix nodes are adding additional layers of anonymity per hop.

**Mixnet-based remailers:** The [Nym](/wiki/Mixnet "Mixnet") network is designed specifically to resist powerful traffic analysis attacks that threaten older remailers and even Tor in some scenarios. Nym uses a layered mixnet architecture with cover traffic to provide strong anonymity for message timing and metadata. Future anonymous email systems are likely to be built directly on top of mixnets like Nym to provide anonymity against nation-state adversaries.[[6]](#cite_note-TorDesign-6)
For any meaningful anonymity, the use of such an integrated network is now considered essential; standalone classical remailers do not provide adequate security.

title: Anonymous remailer
text:
## Web-based mailer

There are also web services that allow users to send anonymous email messages. These services typically do not provide the strong pseudonymity of cryptographic remailers, let alone anonymity, and they are often easier to use. When using a web-based anonymous email service, its reputation and [privacy policy](/wiki/Privacy_policy "Privacy policy") should first be analyzed carefully, since the service stands between senders and recipients. Many such services log the users [IP addresses](/wiki/IP_address "IP address"); others may offer superior privacy but still require trust in the operator.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

title: Anonymous remailer
text:
## Remailer statistics

In most cases, remailers are owned and operated by individuals, and are not as stable as they might ideally be. In fact, remailers can, and have, gone down without warning. It is important to use up-to-date statistics, such as those provided by SEC3[[8]](#cite_note-8) when choosing remailers.

title: Anonymous remailer
section: Remailer abuse and blocking by governments
heading_path: Remailer abuse and blocking by governments
text:
## Remailer abuse and blocking by governments

While most remailers are used responsibly, their pseudonymity has been exploited for illegal activities. A prominent example is the [2012 University of Pittsburgh bomb threats](/wiki/2012_University_of_Pittsburgh_bomb_threats "2012 University of Pittsburgh bomb threats"), where an Anonymous-linked remailer was seized by the [FBI](/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation") after being used to send over 100 threatening emails.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

Some remailers disclaim responsibility for abuse, citing technical and ethical limitations that prevent operators from identifying users.[[10]](#cite_note-DZ-10) Others argue that monitoring for certain abuses would itself be illegal under privacy laws.[[10]](#cite_note-DZ-10)

title: Alice and Bob
text:
Placeholder characters

"Alice & Bob" redirects here. For the company, see [Alice & Bob (company)](/wiki/Alice_%26_Bob_(company) "Alice & Bob (company)").

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Alice-bob-mallory.jpg/250px-Alice-bob-mallory.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Alice-bob-mallory.jpg)

Example scenario where communication between Alice and Bob is intercepted by Mallory

**Alice and Bob** are fictional characters commonly used as [placeholders](/wiki/Placeholder_name "Placeholder name") in discussions about [cryptographic](/wiki/Cryptography "Cryptography") systems and [protocols](/wiki/Cryptographic_protocol "Cryptographic protocol"),[[1]](#cite_note-rfc4949-1) and in other science and engineering literature where there are several participants in a [thought experiment](/wiki/Thought_experiment "Thought experiment"). The Alice and Bob characters were created by [Ron Rivest](/wiki/Ron_Rivest "Ron Rivest"), [Adi Shamir](/wiki/Adi_Shamir "Adi Shamir"), and [Leonard Adleman](/wiki/Leonard_Adleman "Leonard Adleman") in their 1978 paper "A Method for Obtaining Digital Signatures and Public-key Cryptosystems".[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2) Subsequently, they have become common [archetypes](/wiki/Archetype "Archetype") in many scientific and engineering fields, such as [quantum cryptography](/wiki/Quantum_cryptography "Quantum cryptography"), [game theory](/wiki/Game_theory "Game theory") and [physics](/wiki/Physics "Physics").[[3]](#cite_note-3) As the use of Alice and Bob became more widespread, additional characters were added, sometimes with particular meanings. These characters do not have to refer to people; they refer to generic agents which might be different computers or even different programs running on a single computer.

title: Alice and Bob
text:
## Overview

[![Image](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Public_key_shared_secret.svg/250px-Public_key_shared_secret.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Public_key_shared_secret.svg)

An example of an "Alice and Bob" used in cryptography

Alice and Bob are the names of fictional characters used for convenience and to aid comprehension. For example, "How can Bob send a private message M to Alice in a public-key cryptosystem?" is believed to be easier to describe and understand than if the hypothetical people were simply named *A* and *B* as in "How can B send a private message M to A in a public-key cryptosystem?"

The names are conventional, and where relevant may use an alliterative mnemonic such as "Mallory" for "malicious" to associate the name with the typical role of that person.

title: Alice and Bob
text:
## History

Scientific papers about thought experiments with several participants often used letters to identify them: *A*, *B*, *C*, etc.

The first mention of Alice and Bob in the context of cryptography was in [Rivest](/wiki/Ron_Rivest "Ron Rivest"), [Shamir](/wiki/Adi_Shamir "Adi Shamir"), and Adleman's 1978 article "A method for obtaining digital signatures and public-key cryptosystems."[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2) They wrote, "For our scenarios we suppose that A and B (also known as Alice and Bob) are two users of a public-key cryptosystem".[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2): 121 Previous to this article, cryptographers typically referred to message senders and receivers as A and B, or other simple symbols. In fact, in the two previous articles by Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman, introducing the [RSA cryptosystem](/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem) "RSA (cryptosystem)"), there is no mention of Alice and Bob.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5) The choice of the first three names may have come from the film *[Bob & Carol & Ted & Alice](/wiki/Bob_%26_Carol_%26_Ted_%26_Alice "Bob & Carol & Ted & Alice")*.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

title: Alice and Bob
text:
The first mention of Alice and Bob in the context of cryptography was in [Rivest](/wiki/Ron_Rivest "Ron Rivest"), [Shamir](/wiki/Adi_Shamir "Adi Shamir"), and Adleman's 1978 article "A method for obtaining digital signatures and public-key cryptosystems."[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2) They wrote, "For our scenarios we suppose that A and B (also known as Alice and Bob) are two users of a public-key cryptosystem".[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2): 121 Previous to this article, cryptographers typically referred to message senders and receivers as A and B, or other simple symbols. In fact, in the two previous articles by Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman, introducing the [RSA cryptosystem](/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem) "RSA (cryptosystem)"), there is no mention of Alice and Bob.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5) The choice of the first three names may have come from the film *[Bob & Carol & Ted & Alice](/wiki/Bob_%26_Carol_%26_Ted_%26_Alice "Bob & Carol & Ted & Alice")*.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Within a few years, however, references to Alice and Bob in cryptological literature became a common [trope](/wiki/Trope_(literature) "Trope (literature)"). Cryptographers would often begin their academic papers with reference to Alice and Bob. For instance, [Michael Rabin](/wiki/Michael_O._Rabin "Michael O. Rabin") began his 1981 paper, "Bob and Alice each have a secret, SB and SA, respectively, which they want to exchange."[[7]](#cite_note-7) Early on, Alice and Bob were starting to appear in other domains, such as in [Manuel Blum](/wiki/Manuel_Blum "Manuel Blum")'s 1981 article, "Coin Flipping by Telephone: A Protocol for Solving Impossible Problems," which begins, "Alice and Bob want to flip a coin by telephone."[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Within a few years, however, references to Alice and Bob in cryptological literature became a common [trope](/wiki/Trope_(literature) "Trope (literature)"). Cryptographers would often begin their academic papers with reference to Alice and Bob. For instance, [Michael Rabin](/wiki/Michael_O._Rabin "Michael O. Rabin") began his 1981 paper, "Bob and Alice each have a secret, SB and SA, respectively, which they want to exchange."[[7]](#cite_note-7) Early on, Alice and Bob were starting to appear in other domains, such as in [Manuel Blum](/wiki/Manuel_Blum "Manuel Blum")'s 1981 article, "Coin Flipping by Telephone: A Protocol for Solving Impossible Problems," which begins, "Alice and Bob want to flip a coin by telephone."[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Although Alice and Bob were invented with no reference to their personality, authors soon began adding colorful descriptions. In 1983, Blum invented a backstory about a troubled relationship between Alice and Bob, writing, "Alice and Bob, recently divorced, mutually distrustful, still do business together. They live on opposite coasts, communicate mainly by telephone, and use their computers to transact business over the telephone."[[9]](#cite_note-9) In 1984, John Gordon delivered his famous[[10]](#cite_note-10) "After Dinner Speech" about Alice and Bob, which he imagines to be the first "definitive biography of Alice and Bob."[[11]](#cite_note-11)

title: Alice and Bob
text:
Although Alice and Bob were invented with no reference to their personality, authors soon began adding colorful descriptions. In 1983, Blum invented a backstory about a troubled relationship between Alice and Bob, writing, "Alice and Bob, recently divorced, mutually distrustful, still do business together. They live on opposite coasts, communicate mainly by telephone, and use their computers to transact business over the telephone."[[9]](#cite_note-9) In 1984, John Gordon delivered his famous[[10]](#cite_note-10) "After Dinner Speech" about Alice and Bob, which he imagines to be the first "definitive biography of Alice and Bob."[[11]](#cite_note-11)

In addition to adding backstories and personalities to Alice and Bob, authors soon added other characters, with their own personalities. The first to be added was Eve, the "eavesdropper." Eve was invented in 1988 by Charles Bennet, Gilles Brassard, and Jean-Marc Robert, in their paper, "Privacy Amplification by Public Discussion."[[12]](#cite_note-12) In [Bruce Schneier](/wiki/Bruce_Schneier "Bruce Schneier")'s book *Applied Cryptography*, other characters are listed.[[13]](#cite_note-13)
