text: ## Cast of characters

title: Alice and Bob
text:
### Cryptographic systems

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| [![icon](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg) | This section **needs [more citations](/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Please help [improve this section](/wiki/Special:EditPage/Alice_and_Bob "Special:EditPage/Alice and Bob") by [adding citations to reliable sources](/wiki/Help:Referencing_for_beginners "Help:Referencing for beginners"). Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability"). *(May 2023)* *([Learn how and when to remove this message](/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))* |

The most common characters are Alice and Bob. Eve, Mallory, and Trent are also common names, and have fairly well-established "personalities" (or functions). The names often use alliterative mnemonics (for example, Eve, "eavesdropper"; Mallory, "malicious") where different players have different motives. Other names are much less common and more flexible in use. Sometimes the genders are alternated: Alice, Bob, Carol, Dave, Eve, etc.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

title: Alice and Bob
text:
The most common characters are Alice and Bob. Eve, Mallory, and Trent are also common names, and have fairly well-established "personalities" (or functions). The names often use alliterative mnemonics (for example, Eve, "eavesdropper"; Mallory, "malicious") where different players have different motives. Other names are much less common and more flexible in use. Sometimes the genders are alternated: Alice, Bob, Carol, Dave, Eve, etc.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| *Alice* and *Bob* | The original, generic characters. Generally, Alice and Bob want to exchange a message or cryptographic key. |
| *Carol*, *Carlos* or *Charlie* | A generic third participant. |
| *Chuck* or *Chad* | A third participant, usually of malicious intent.[[15]](#cite_note-15) |
| *Craig* | A *[password cracker](/wiki/Password_cracking "Password cracking"),* often encountered in situations with stored passwords. |
| *Dan*, *Dave* or *David* | A generic fourth participant. |
| *Erin* | A generic fifth participant, but rarely used, as "E" is usually reserved for Eve. |
| *Eve* or *Yves* | An *[eavesdropper](/wiki/Eavesdropping "Eavesdropping")*, who is usually a passive attacker. While they can listen in on messages between Alice and Bob, they cannot modify them. In [quantum cryptography](/wiki/Quantum_cryptography "Quantum cryptography"), Eve may also represent the *environment*.[*[clarification needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")*] |
| *Faythe* | A *trusted [advisor](/wiki/Adviser "Adviser")*, courier or intermediary. Faythe is used infrequently, and is associated with *faith* and *faithfulness*. Faythe may be a repository of key service or courier of shared secrets.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] |
| *Frank* | A generic sixth participant. |
| *Grace* | A *government representative*. For example, Grace may try to force Alice or Bob to implement backdoors in their protocols. Grace may also deliberately weaken standards.[[16]](#cite_note-16) |
| *Heidi* | A *mischievous designer* for cryptographic standards, but rarely used.[[17]](#cite_note-17) |
| *Ivan* | An *issuer*, mentioned first by Ian Grigg in the context of [Ricardian contracts](/wiki/Ricardian_contract "Ricardian contract").[[18]](#cite_note-18) |

title: Alice and Bob
text:
|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| *Judy* | A *judge* who may be called upon to resolve a potential dispute between participants. See [Judge Judy](/wiki/Judge_Judy "Judge Judy"). |
| *Mallory*[[19]](#cite_note-Schneier1996-19)[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21) or (less commonly) *Mallet*[[22]](#cite_note-Schneier1994-22)[[23]](#cite_note-Perkins2000-23)[[24]](#cite_note-LaMacchia2002-24)[[25]](#cite_note-Dolev2009-25) or *Darth*[[26]](#cite_note-Stallings1998-26) | A *malicious attacker*. Associated with Trudy, an *intruder*. Unlike the passive Eve, Mallory is an active attacker (often used in [man-in-the-middle attacks](/wiki/Man-in-the-middle_attack "Man-in-the-middle attack")), who can modify messages, substitute messages, or replay old messages. The difficulty of securing a system against a Mallory is much greater than against an Eve. |
| *Michael* or *Mike* | Used as an alternative to the eavesdropper Eve, from *[microphone](/wiki/Microphone "Microphone")*. |
| *Niaj* | Used as an alternative to the eavesdropper Eve in several South Asian nations.[[27]](#cite_note-27) |
| *Olivia* | An *[oracle](/wiki/Oracle_machine "Oracle machine")*, who responds to queries from other participants. Olivia often acts as a "[black box](/wiki/Black_box "Black box")" with some concealed state or information, or as a [random oracle](/wiki/Random_oracle "Random oracle"). |
| *Oscar* | An *opponent*, similar to Mallory, but not necessarily malicious. |
| *Peggy* or *Pat* | A *prover*, who interacts with the *verifier* to show that the intended transaction has actually taken place. Peggy is often found in [zero-knowledge proofs](/wiki/Zero-knowledge_proof "Zero-knowledge proof"). |

title: Alice and Bob
text:
|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| *Rupert* | A *repudiator* who appears for interactions that desire [non-repudiation](/wiki/Non-repudiation "Non-repudiation"). |
| *Sybil* | A *[pseudonymous](/wiki/Pseudonym "Pseudonym") attacker*, who usually uses a large number of identities. For example, Sybil may attempt to subvert a [reputation system](/wiki/Reputation_system "Reputation system"). See [Sybil attack](/wiki/Sybil_attack "Sybil attack"). |
| *Trent* or *Ted* | A *trusted [arbitrator](/wiki/Arbitral_tribunal "Arbitral tribunal")*, who acts as a [neutral third party](/wiki/Trusted_third_party "Trusted third party"). |
| *Trudy* | An *intruder*. |
| *Victor*[[19]](#cite_note-Schneier1996-19) or *Vanna*[[28]](#cite_note-28) | *A verifier*, who requires proof from the *prover*. |
| *Walter* | A *[warden](/wiki/Prison_warden "Prison warden")*, who may guard Alice and Bob. |
| *Wendy* | A *[whistleblower](/wiki/Whistleblower "Whistleblower")*, who is an insider with privileged access capable of divulging information. |

title: Alice and Bob
text:
### Interactive proof systems

For [interactive proof systems](/wiki/Interactive_proof_system "Interactive proof system") there are other characters:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| *Arthur* and *Merlin* | Merlin provides answers, and Arthur asks questions.[[29]](#cite_note-29) Merlin has unbounded computational ability (like the wizard [Merlin](/wiki/Merlin "Merlin")). In interactive proof systems, Merlin claims the truth of a statement, and Arthur (like [King Arthur](/wiki/King_Arthur "King Arthur")), questions him to verify the claim. |
| *Paul* and *Carole* | Paul asks questions, and Carole provides answers. In the solution of the [Twenty Questions](/wiki/Twenty_Questions "Twenty Questions") problem,[[30]](#cite_note-30) Paul (standing in for [Paul Erdős](/wiki/Paul_Erd%C5%91s "Paul Erdős")) asked questions and Carole (an [anagram](/wiki/Anagram "Anagram") of "[oracle](/wiki/Oracle "Oracle")") answered them. Paul and Carole were also used in [combinatorial games](/wiki/Combinatorial_game_theory "Combinatorial game theory"), in the roles of pusher and chooser.[[31]](#cite_note-31) |
| *Arthur* and *Bertha* | Arthur is the "left", "black", or "vertical" player, and Bertha is the "right", "white", or "horizontal" player in a [combinatorial game](/wiki/Combinatorial_game_theory "Combinatorial game theory"). Additionally, Arthur, given the same outcome, prefers a game to take the fewest moves, while Bertha prefers a game to take the most moves.[[32]](#cite_note-32) |

title: Alice and Bob
text:
### Physics

The names Alice and Bob are often used to name the participants in thought experiments in physics.[[33]](#cite_note-33)[[34]](#cite_note-34) More alphabetical names, usually of alternating gender, are used as required, e.g. "Alice and Bob (and Carol and Dave and Eve)".[[35]](#cite_note-35)

In experiments involving robotic systems, the terms "Alice Robot" and "Bob Robot" refer to mobile platforms responsible for transmitting quantum information and receiving it with quantum detectors, respectively, within the context of the field of [quantum robotics](/wiki/Quantum_robotics "Quantum robotics").[[36]](#cite_note-36)[[37]](#cite_note-37)[[38]](#cite_note-38)[[39]](#cite_note-39)[[40]](#cite_note-40)[[41]](#cite_note-41)

**Bitcoin Satoshi Vision (BSV)** is a cryptocurrency that is a [hard fork](/wiki/Hard_fork "Hard fork") of [Bitcoin Cash](/wiki/Bitcoin_Cash "Bitcoin Cash").[[1]](#cite_note-51attack-1) Bitcoin Satoshi Vision was created in November 2018 by a group of individuals led by [Craig Steven Wright](/wiki/Craig_Steven_Wright "Craig Steven Wright"), who has claimed since 2015 to be [Satoshi Nakamoto](/wiki/Satoshi_Nakamoto "Satoshi Nakamoto"), the creator of the original bitcoin.[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-CNBCSV-3)

title: Bitcoin Satoshi Vision
text: ## History

title: Bitcoin Satoshi Vision
text:
### 2018 split from Bitcoin Cash

On 15 November 2018, a hard fork chain split of Bitcoin Cash occurred between two rival factions called Bitcoin Cash and Bitcoin SV.[[4]](#cite_note-Bloom17112018-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5) On 15 November 2018 Bitcoin Cash traded at about [$](/wiki/US_dollar "US dollar")289, and Bitcoin SV traded at about $96.50, down from $425.01 on 14 November for the un-split Bitcoin Cash.[[6]](#cite_note-Bloom15112018-6)

The split originated from what was described as a "civil war" in two competing Bitcoin Cash camps. The first camp, supported by entrepreneur [Roger Ver](/wiki/Roger_Ver "Roger Ver") and [Jihan Wu](/wiki/Jihan_Wu "Jihan Wu") of [Bitmain](/wiki/Bitmain "Bitmain"), promoted the software entitled Bitcoin ABC (short for Adjustable Blocksize Cap), which would maintain the block size at 32 [MB](/wiki/Megabyte "Megabyte").[[7]](#cite_note-SCMP20181115-7) The second camp led by [Craig Steven Wright](/wiki/Craig_Steven_Wright "Craig Steven Wright") and billionaire [Calvin Ayre](/wiki/Calvin_Ayre "Calvin Ayre") put forth a competing software version Bitcoin SV, short for "Bitcoin Satoshi Vision", which would increase the block size limit to 128 MB.[[4]](#cite_note-Bloom17112018-4)[[7]](#cite_note-SCMP20181115-7)

title: Bitcoin Satoshi Vision
text:
### 2019 de-listing from Binance

In April 2019, an online feud broke out between those who supported the claims of Bitcoin SV supporter Craig Wright that he was Satoshi Nakamoto, and those who did not.[[8]](#cite_note-binancedelist-8) The feud resulted in cryptocurrency exchange [Binance](/wiki/Binance "Binance") de-listing Bitcoin SV from their platform, stating that:[[8]](#cite_note-binancedelist-8)

> At Binance, we periodically review each digital asset we list to ensure that it continues to meet the high level of standard we expect. When a coin or token no longer meets this standard, or the industry changes, we conduct a more in-depth review and potentially delist it. We believe this best protects all of our users.
>
> When we conduct these reviews, we consider a variety of factors. Here are some that drive whether we decide to delist a digital asset:
>
> - Commitment of team to project
> - Level and quality of development activity
> - Network / smart contract stability
> - Level of public communication[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]
> - Responsiveness to our periodic due diligence requests
> - Evidence of unethical / fraudulent conduct
> - Contribution to a healthy and sustainable crypto ecosystem

title: Bitcoin Satoshi Vision
text:
### 2021 network attack

In August 2021, Bitcoin SV suffered a [51% attack](/wiki/51%25_attack "51% attack"), after previously suffering attacks in June and July of the same year.[[1]](#cite_note-51attack-1) Such an attack involves [cryptocurrency miners](/wiki/Cryptominer "Cryptominer") gaining control of more than half of a network's computing power; these kinds of network attacks have the goal of preventing new transactions from gaining confirmations, allowing the attackers to [double-spend](/wiki/Double-spending "Double-spending") coins. Adam James, senior editor at OKEx Insights claimed that "In the intermediate term, the attack has seemingly somewhat-negligible impact on its current price action," however "Faith in [Bitcoin SV] will likely be reduced following the incident."[[1]](#cite_note-51attack-1)

title: Bitcoin Satoshi Vision
text:
### 2024 high court ruling

In March 2024, Mr Justice [James Mellor](/wiki/James_Mellor_(judge) "James Mellor (judge)") in the British [High Court of Justice](/wiki/High_Court_of_Justice "High Court of Justice") ruled that Wright is not Satoshi Nakamoto.[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10)

title: Serge Belamant
text:
South African entrepreneur (born 1953)

| Serge Christian Pierre Belamant | |
| --- | --- |
| Born | (1953-09-22) September 22, 1953 (age 72)  Tulle, France |
| Occupations | Entrepreneur, inventor |
| Known for | Universal Electronic Payment System (UEPS); Chip Offline Pre-authorised Card (COPAC) |
| Title | Founder of Net1 UEPS Technologies; Co-founder & chair of Zilch |

**Serge Belamant** (born 1953) is a French-born South African entrepreneur best known for designing the Universal Electronic [Payment System](/wiki/Payment_system "Payment system") (UEPS) and the Chip Offline Pre-authorised Card (COPAC).[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)

He founded the cash-payments company Net1 UEPS Technologies in 1989, led it through dual listings on the [NASDAQ](/wiki/NASDAQ "NASDAQ") and the [Johannesburg Stock Exchange](/wiki/Johannesburg_Stock_Exchange "Johannesburg Stock Exchange"), and oversaw the contentious welfare-payments contract with the South African Social Security Agency (SASSA) until his retirement in 2017.[[3]](#cite_note-3) Since 2018 he has been non-executive chair of London-based buy-now-pay-later fintech Zilch.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

title: Serge Belamant
text:
## Early life and education

Belamant moved from France to South Africa with his family in 1967 and matriculated from Highlands North Boys' High School, Johannesburg.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] In 1972 he entered the [University of the Witwatersrand](/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand "University of the Witwatersrand") to study civil engineering but switched to computer science and [applied mathematics](/wiki/Applied_mathematics "Applied mathematics") in his second year. He left the university without a degree and later took short courses in information systems at the [University of South Africa](/wiki/University_of_South_Africa "University of South Africa") (UNISA).[[4]](#cite_note-4)

title: Serge Belamant
text:
## Early career and SASWITCH (1981–1989)

Belamant worked for [Control Data Corporation](/wiki/Control_Data_Corporation "Control Data Corporation") as a systems analyst for a decade before joining SASWITCH Ltd in 1985.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] Economic sanctions had left the consortium's national ATM network dependent on unsupported Christian Rovsing computers.[[5]](#cite_note-BizNewsInterview-5) Belamant led a rebuild on fault-tolerant Stratus hardware and wrote protocol-translation software that allowed fourteen banks to connect without altering their host systems.[[6]](#cite_note-CompCom2008-6)

By 1988 SASWITCH was handling about three million ATM transactions a month, according to the Competition Commission.[[5]](#cite_note-BizNewsInterview-5) The switch—now run by BankservAfrica—remains the backbone of South Africa's shared ATM network.[[7]](#cite_note-:2-7)

title: Serge Belamant
text: ## Net1 UEPS Technologies (1989–2017)

title: Serge Belamant
text:
### Founding and UEPS

In 1989, Serge Belamant developed the Universal Electronic Payment System (UEPS), enabling secure, real-time transactions even in areas with limited connectivity. In the same year, he founded NET1 UEPS Technologies Inc., serving as its CEO and Director.[[7]](#cite_note-:2-7)

title: Serge Belamant
text:
### COPAC for VISA

In 1995, VISA tasked Belamant with designing the Chip Offline Pre-authorized Card (COPAC), a technology still widely used in chip-enabled credit and debit cards.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] A year later, he listed his company APLITEC (Applied Technology Holdings Limited) on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

title: Serge Belamant
text:
### Listings and acquisitions

In 1999, Belamant acquired Cash Payment Services (CPS) from First National Bank of South Africa, modernizing its welfare payment system to serve millions in rural areas.[[9]](#cite_note-9) In 2005, he led NET1 Technologies to an IPO, listing it as NET1 UEPS Technologies Inc. on the Nasdaq. A secondary listing on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) followed in 2008.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

title: Serge Belamant
text:
### SASSA contract

Under Belamant's leadership, NET1 managed welfare payments for the South African Social Security Agency (SASSA), handling payments for over 10 million beneficiaries monthly.[[11]](#cite_note-11) Despite criticism over handling the SASSA contract, investigations by the [U.S. Department of Justice](/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice") and the South African Constitutional Court found no wrongdoing.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

title: Serge Belamant
text:
## Zilch (2018–present)

Belamant co-founded London-based "buy-now-pay-later" firm Zilch Technology in 2018 and serves as non-executive chair.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) Zilch reported £145 million in annual-recurring revenue and 4.5 million customers in January 2025.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

title: Serge Belamant
text:
## Patents

Belamant is listed as inventor on more than a dozen payment-security patents, including:

- "Funds transfer system" (US RE36,788, 2000) – the basis for UEPS.[[14]](#cite_note-14)
- "Financial transactions with a varying PIN" (WO 2014/037869, 2014).[[15]](#cite_note-15)
